title: Dreaming of Wings
summary: Long ago, people watched birds and wished they could fly too. They told stories about magic wings, flew silk kites in China, and a few brave people even jumped off towers wearing feathers. They got hurt, but they started the greatest adventure in the sky!

sections.heading: Why Everyone Envied the Birds
paragraphs: Imagine sitting on a hillside four thousand years ago. You have no car, no bicycle and no map. To get anywhere you walk, ride a donkey or paddle a boat. A river in front of you might take a whole day to cross. A mountain might take a week. Then a hawk lifts off a rock, tilts its wings, and in a few seconds it is gliding over the river and circling above the mountain as if neither of them existed.

No wonder people were jealous. Birds could do things that seemed like pure magic. A swallow can twist and dart after insects faster than you can follow it with your eyes. An eagle can hang almost still in the wind, wings spread, hardly flapping at all. Geese fly in great V shapes across whole continents every autumn and come back every spring. For a human stuck on the ground, birds were the ultimate symbol of freedom.

Flying would also have been incredibly useful. A person who could fly could see enemies coming from far away, find lost animals, carry messages across a valley, or escape from a dangerous place. Kings and generals dreamed about it for war. Poets dreamed about it for the feeling of floating among the clouds. Ordinary farmers probably just dreamed about getting to the market faster.

But wanting to fly and knowing HOW to fly are two very different things. For thousands of years, nobody understood what was really happening when a bird stayed up in the air. People did not know that air is a real substance made of countless tiny particles that push on everything they touch. They did not know about lift, drag or balance. So, for a very long time, the dream of flight lived mostly in stories.

In this first part of our journey we will visit those stories, then travel to ancient China, where people really did put objects into the sky using wind and string. Finally we will meet two brave men, one in Spain and one in England, who are said to have strapped on wings and jumped. Their stories were written down long after they happened, so we have to be careful detectives about what is certain and what is not. That kind of careful thinking, as you will see, is exactly what humans needed before they could truly fly.

sections.heading: Wings in the Old Stories
paragraphs: The most famous flying story in the world comes from ancient Greece. It is a myth, which means a traditional story that people told to explain the world or teach a lesson, not a record of something that really happened. It is the tale of Daedalus and his son Icarus.

In the legend, Daedalus was a brilliant craftsman from Athens. He worked for King Minos on the island of Crete and built him a giant maze called the Labyrinth, where a monster called the Minotaur, half man and half bull, was kept. Later the king grew angry with Daedalus and would not let him and his son leave the island. Crete is surrounded by sea, and the king controlled the ships. So Daedalus looked up. If they could not escape by land or by water, they would escape by air.

Daedalus collected feathers and fastened them together with thread and beeswax, making two pairs of wings shaped like a bird's. Before they took off, he gave Icarus a warning. Do not fly too low, or the spray from the sea will soak the feathers and make them heavy. Do not fly too high, or the heat of the Sun will melt the wax. Stay in the middle.

At first all went well. But Icarus loved the feeling of soaring and climbed higher and higher. In the story, the Sun's heat softened the wax, the feathers came loose, and Icarus fell into the sea and drowned. His heartbroken father named the nearby island Icaria, and the waters there are still called the Icarian Sea. The Roman poet Ovid told this story in great detail in his long poem called the Metamorphoses, written about 2,000 years ago, and artists have painted it ever since. In one famous painting, Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, made in the 1500s and usually linked to the Flemish artist Pieter Bruegel the Elder, a farmer keeps ploughing his field while poor Icarus is just a tiny pair of legs splashing into the sea in the corner.

Today people still say someone is 'flying too close to the Sun' when they take a big risk out of too much confidence. Of course, real science tells us the story could never happen the way it is told. The higher you climb in the sky, the COLDER it gets, not warmer. Jet airliners fly through air that is far below freezing. But myths are not meant to be science. This one is about ambition, warnings and listening to good advice.

Greece was not the only place with flying legends. A Persian legend tells of a king named Kay Kavus who tied hungry eagles to his throne and dangled meat above them, so that as they flew up toward the food they carried the throne into the sky. Another old tale says Alexander the Great was carried aloft in a basket pulled by griffins, imaginary creatures that were part eagle and part lion. Ancient Indian writings describe vimanas, magnificent flying palaces or chariots used by gods and heroes. In Greek myths, the messenger god Hermes zipped around in winged sandals. A British legend even claims that an ancient king named Bladud made himself wings and died trying to fly over a city.

There are also stories that sound a little more like engineering. A Greek thinker named Archytas of Taranto, who lived around 400 BCE, is said to have built a wooden pigeon that could move through the air, perhaps pushed by a puff of steam and held on a wire or pivot. Nobody knows what it really looked like, or if it existed at all. It may simply be a legend that grew over the centuries.

All these stories have something in common. They show that people from many cultures, on many continents, shared the same dream. And almost all of them imagined flight the same way: either borrowing the power of real birds, or copying birds by wearing wings. That idea would turn out to be a trap, as we will see at the end of this part.

sections.heading: Silk, Bamboo and the Wind: China's First Kites
paragraphs: While stories of feathered wings were being told around the Mediterranean, people in China were doing something remarkable. They were putting real objects into the sky and keeping them there. These objects were kites.

Many historians think the kite may be the very first human-made aircraft that was heavier than air, meaning it stays up even though it weighs more than the air it pushes aside. That makes the kite a distant great-great-grandparent of every airplane and glider. Kites in China are often said to date back more than 2,000 years, and some writers place them as early as the 400s BCE.

Chinese tradition links the first kites to two famous figures. One was Mozi, a philosopher and engineer who taught that people should care for everyone equally. The other was Lu Ban, a legendary master carpenter who is still honoured as the patron of builders and woodworkers in China. One old story says Mozi spent three years making a bird out of wood that flew for a day before breaking. Another says Lu Ban carved a wooden magpie that could stay aloft. These are traditions passed down in ancient books, not proven history. Nobody has dug up a 2,400-year-old kite to check. But the stories tell us something important: in China, building things that rode the wind was thought of as a skill for clever craftsmen.

The earliest kites were said to be made of wood. Later, kite makers used a combination that turned out to be almost perfect. For the frame they used bamboo, which is light, strong and springy, so it bends in a gust instead of snapping. For the sail they used silk, a smooth, thin fabric that is very strong for its weight. For the flying line they used fine silk thread, which could hold a strong pull without breaking. After paper was invented in China during the Han dynasty (which began in 206 BCE), paper kites became popular too, because paper was cheaper than silk. In Chinese, an old word for kite meant 'paper hawk'.

How does a kite actually fly? When the wind blows against the tilted face of a kite, the air is pushed downward and backward. The air pushes back on the kite, upward and backward, just as a wall pushes back on you when you lean on it. The string holds the kite in place, so instead of being blown away, it climbs. The tail helps keep the kite pointing the right way, like the feathers on an arrow. Without realising it, ancient kite makers had discovered several of the key ideas of flight: a tilted surface, moving air, and the need for balance and steadiness.

Over the centuries Chinese kites became works of art. They were painted with dragons, birds, butterflies and heroes from old stories. By the Tang dynasty (618 to 907 CE), people were attaching small bamboo pipes and whistles to kites so that they hummed and sang in the wind. That is why one modern Chinese word for kite, fengzheng, comes from the name of a stringed musical instrument: the kite was literally a harp played by the wind.

sections.heading: Kites at Work: Signals, Wind and Lifting People
paragraphs: Kites in ancient China were not only toys. Old Chinese writings describe them being used for serious jobs: measuring distances, testing the wind, sending signals and carrying messages. Picture an army camped on a plain. A kite rising above the camp could be seen for kilometres, and its colour or shape could tell friendly troops something without anyone shouting a word. A kite also showed which way the wind was blowing and roughly how strong it was, which mattered to sailors, soldiers and anyone planning to light a fire.

One story tells how a kite was used in a siege around 549 CE, when a city was surrounded by enemies. A kite carried a message out over the enemy lines, asking for rescue. Whether or not help arrived in time, the idea was clever: the sky was the one road the enemy could not block.

A darker set of stories shows that people in China also understood that kites could lift something as heavy as a human being. According to Chinese histories written centuries later, a cruel ruler named Gao Yang, emperor of a kingdom called Northern Qi, forced prisoners to jump from a high tower attached to large kites or bamboo mats, as a kind of punishment, around the year 559 CE. Most of them did not survive. But one, a prince named Yuan Huangtou, is recorded as gliding all the way to a road called the Purple Way, about 2.5 kilometres away, and landing alive. It is a sad story about how prisoners were treated, and historians cannot check every detail. But if it is even partly true, it would be one of the earliest reports of a person being carried through the air by a wing-like surface.

Much later, the Italian traveller Marco Polo, who visited China in the late 1200s, wrote about sailors who tied a man to a large kite before a voyage. They watched how the kite flew: if it rose straight and high, the voyage would be lucky; if it would not climb, the ship stayed in port. Polo noted how dangerous and unkind this was for the man on the kite. Stories like his helped carry news of kites to Europe, though Europeans would not take kites seriously as a scientific tool for hundreds of years.

China gave the world other early flying objects too. Small paper hot-air lanterns, now called sky lanterns, are believed to go back a very long time in China. A famous general named Zhuge Liang, who lived from 181 to 234 CE, is said to have used them to send signals or to startle enemy troops, which is why they are sometimes called Kongming lanterns after his nickname. These lanterns worked like tiny hot-air balloons: a small flame heated the air inside a paper bag, and the warm, lighter air floated the lantern upward. Chinese children also played with a toy sometimes called the bamboo-copter, a stick with little blades on top that whirled up into the air when you spun it between your palms. Hundreds of years later, a toy very much like it would delight two young brothers in Ohio, as you will read in Part 6.

Notice something about all of these Chinese inventions. A kite, a sky lantern and a bamboo-copter do not flap. They use wind, warm air or spinning blades. In a way, these toys and tools were closer to how real aircraft would one day fly than any pair of feathered wings.

sections.heading: The Tower Jumpers: Abbas ibn Firnas of Córdoba
paragraphs: Across the world, people kept trying the most obvious idea of all: strap on wings, find something high, and jump. Historians call these brave and often unlucky people the 'tower jumpers'. Most of them were badly hurt. Very few left reliable records. But a couple of their stories became famous.

One comes from Córdoba, in what is now southern Spain. About 1,200 years ago, Córdoba was one of the largest and most splendid cities in Europe. It was the capital of al-Andalus, the part of Spain ruled by Muslim emirs, and it had libraries, mosques, gardens, paved streets and scholars studying mathematics, medicine, music and the stars.

Among those scholars was Abbas ibn Firnas, who lived from about 810 to 887. He was what we call a polymath, a person who is expert in many different subjects. He was a poet and musician at the emir's court, an astronomer and an inventor. He is said to have designed a water clock, built a device that showed the movements of the planets and stars, found a way to cut rock crystal (a kind of clear quartz) in Spain instead of sending it all the way to Egypt, and worked on making clear glass.

According to the story, Abbas ibn Firnas covered himself in feathers, fixed wings to his arms, and launched himself from a high place. Witnesses said he glided a long way through the air before coming down. But the landing went badly. He crashed hard and hurt his back. Afterwards he is said to have explained what went wrong: he had not given himself a tail. Birds, he realised, use their tails to slow down and land gently, and he had none.
That explanation is actually very smart. A tail helps any flying thing stay steady and control its landing. Modern airplanes all have tail surfaces for exactly that reason.

But here is where we must be good history detectives. The main account of the flight was written by a historian named al-Maqqari, who died in 1632. That means he was writing roughly 750 years after Abbas ibn Firnas lived. Al-Maqqari did not explain where he found all his details, and no full eyewitness description has survived. The flight is often dated to around 875, but nobody knows the exact year. One interesting clue does exist: al-Maqqari quoted a poem by a court poet named Mu'min ibn Said, who lived at the same time as Abbas ibn Firnas, saying that he 'flew faster than the phoenix', a mythical bird. Because the verse sounds like teasing, some historians think it may be a joke about a real event. So something probably did happen, but how far he glided and exactly what his wings looked like are uncertain.

Abbas ibn Firnas is still remembered with pride. In 1973 a statue of him was put up near Baghdad International Airport in Iraq. In 1976, astronomers named a crater on the Moon after him. And in 2011 a bridge in Córdoba was named in his honour. Remember, though: he did not build an airplane, and nothing he made had an engine or could be steered like an aircraft. He was a brave early experimenter, one of the very first people we know by name who tried to ride the air.

sections.heading: Eilmer, the Flying Monk of Malmesbury
paragraphs: About a hundred and thirty years later, and over 1,500 kilometres to the north, another man had the same idea. His name was Eilmer, and he was a Benedictine monk at Malmesbury Abbey, a great stone monastery in the south-west of England. His name is sometimes written Elmer, Æthelmær or even Oliver.

Imagine the scene. It is early in the 1000s, a time when England was ruled by Anglo-Saxon kings and Vikings were still raiding the coasts. The abbey is the tallest building for miles. Young Eilmer, who had read the old story of Daedalus, has made himself a pair of wings and fastened them to his hands and feet. He climbs to the top of a tower, waits for a breeze, and leaps.

According to the account, the wind caught his wings and carried him forward. He glided for more than a furlong, an old English measurement equal to about 200 metres. That is about two football pitches! Some modern writers have estimated he might have been in the air for around 15 seconds. Then something went wrong. Perhaps the wind swirled around the buildings, or perhaps he panicked. He lost control, fell, and broke both his legs. He was lame, meaning he limped, for the rest of his life.

And what did Eilmer say had gone wrong? Amazingly, the same thing as Abbas ibn Firnas: he had forgotten to give himself a tail. There is no proof that Eilmer had ever heard of the man in Córdoba, so it seems that two people, far apart, reached the same smart conclusion from their painful crashes.

How do we know any of this? Almost everything comes from one writer: William of Malmesbury, a monk and one of the best historians of medieval England. He wrote a big history of the English kings around the year 1125, about a hundred years after the flight. William lived in the same abbey and probably heard the story from older monks who had known Eilmer when he was an old man. That makes the account better than a random legend, but it is still second-hand, so we cannot be completely sure of the distance or the details. Historians usually say Eilmer flew 'around 1010', because the exact year is not recorded.

Eilmer is remembered for something else too. William wrote that when a bright comet appeared in the sky in 1066, the elderly Eilmer saw it and cried out that it was a sign of disaster for England. Later that year, England was conquered by William of Normandy at the Battle of Hastings. That comet is the one we now call Halley's Comet. It even appears on the famous Bayeux Tapestry.

Today, Malmesbury Abbey has a stained-glass window, put in in 1920, that shows Eilmer holding his wings. A lane in the town, traditionally said to be near where he landed, is called Olivers Lane. Not bad for a monk who broke both his legs!

sections.heading: The Big Mistake: Copying the Flapping Bird
paragraphs: Abbas ibn Firnas and Eilmer were not the only tower jumpers. Old Chinese histories say that around the first century CE, a man was dressed in bird feathers and is reported to have glided about 100 metres during the reign of the ruler Wang Mang. Over the following centuries, more people in Europe and the Middle East tried feathered cloaks, wooden wings and stiff capes. Many crashed. Some died. Almost none of them left behind notes that anyone else could learn from.

Why did they keep failing? The biggest reason is that they were copying the wrong thing. When we watch a bird, the most obvious thing it does is flap. So most dreamers believed that flapping was the secret, and that if a person could just flap big enough wings, they would rise into the sky. But flapping is actually one of the hardest ways to fly, and it is very hard to copy.

A bird's body is a marvel of lightweight engineering. Many bird bones are hollow, with thin struts inside like the beams of a bridge. Their feathers are incredibly light for their size. And their chest muscles, which power the downstroke of the wing, are enormous compared with the rest of the body. In a pigeon, the flight muscles make up a very large share of its whole weight. Our arm and chest muscles are much smaller compared with our heavy bodies. A person flapping homemade wings simply cannot produce enough power to lift themselves. Scientists would not prove this with numbers until the 1600s, as you will see in the next part.

There was a second problem: nobody understood the air itself. Ancient and medieval people knew that wind could push sails and turn windmills, but they did not have a clear idea that a moving wing could create an upward push called lift. They did not know about drag, the air resistance that slows things down. And they did not understand balance and control: how a flying thing keeps from tipping over, and how it can be steered. That is why the 'forgot the tail' explanations of Abbas ibn Firnas and Eilmer are so interesting. Both men had stumbled onto the idea of stability, but they had no way to study it properly.

Look back at the kite. It does not flap at all. It holds a fixed, tilted surface into moving air, and it uses a tail for steadiness. In a strange way, the Chinese kite makers were closer to the answer than the brave men leaping from towers. Many centuries later, an English inventor would look at the problem in exactly this way: stop flapping, keep the wing still, and find another way to push it forward. But that story belongs to Part 3.

Another lesson from the tower jumpers is about sharing knowledge. Each jumper mostly started from scratch. There were no journals, no test reports and no diagrams passed from one inventor to the next. When experimenters finally began writing down careful measurements and sharing them, progress sped up enormously.

By around the year 1100, then, humanity had beautiful myths, clever kites, sky lanterns and a few painful tower jumps. What it did not have was understanding. Dreaming was not enough. Someone needed to study birds and air the way a scientist would: watching, measuring, drawing and asking why. About four hundred years later, in Renaissance Italy, a painter with a notebook full of backwards handwriting began to do exactly that. His name was Leonardo da Vinci.

deepDive: Historians of early flight face a basic problem: almost every story before about 1500 comes from sources written long after the event. Eilmer's flight is known mainly from William of Malmesbury's Gesta regum Anglorum (about 1125), roughly a century later, though William's local connection to the abbey gives it some weight. Abbas ibn Firnas is worse off: the main account comes from al-Maqqari in the 1600s, about seven centuries later, with only a contemporary poem as supporting evidence. The American historian of technology Lynn White Jr. took both stories seriously and argued that they show genuine gliding experiments, while others warn that later writers liked to tell dramatic tales about clever men. The honest position is that both men probably attempted something like a glide, and both probably crashed, but distances and details cannot be verified. The physics behind their 'forgot the tail' explanations is real. A stable aircraft needs its centre of lift and its centre of gravity arranged so that, if the nose pitches up or down, the air pushes it back toward level flight. A tail placed well behind the wing does this, the way the fletching on an arrow keeps the point forward. Without one, a human with wings tends to pitch and tumble, especially near the ground where gusts and turbulence are strongest. Kites are also scientifically important. A kite is a heavier-than-air craft held at an angle of attack, the angle between its surface and the wind, and kept stable by its bridle and tail. Joseph Needham, the great historian of Chinese science, argued that Chinese kites, sky lanterns and the spinning bamboo-copter toy were among the first technologies to use aerodynamic and buoyant forces. When kites became common in Europe, and later when George Cayley experimented with kite-shaped wings and Lawrence Hargrave built box kites, they formed a direct link from ancient Chinese toys to the first airplanes. Finally, the human-muscle problem is about power-to-weight ratio. A fit person can produce only a few hundred watts for long, while their body is heavy. Human-powered aircraft were finally flown in the 1970s, but only with huge, ultra-light wings built from modern materials and pedals driving a propeller, not flapping arms.
funFact: Abbas ibn Firnas, the scholar who reportedly glided over Córdoba around 1,150 years ago, has a crater on the Moon named after him.

check.q: According to the stories, what did both Abbas ibn Firnas and Eilmer of Malmesbury say they had forgotten to give themselves?
